name: Cold compress for red eyes

lead: Holding something cold against the eyelids is a common quick fix for puffy or red-looking eyes. People use it before going out for a fresher look that lasts a while.

Cold on the face causes vasoconstriction in physiology tests, which is the usual reasoning given for reduced redness and swelling. One small trial examined cold compresses for induced allergic eye symptoms; none have measured cosmetic whiteness.

paras: Users rest a chilled cloth, gel pack or cold spoons on closed lids for a few minutes, often in the morning or just before an event. The effect is described as temporary.

Clinical references list many causes of red eye, some urgent such as angle-closure glaucoma, so persistent or painful redness is a medical matter. Ice should not be pressed directly on the skin for long.

angle.text: A chilled cloth on the closed lids narrows blood vessels and cuts puffiness and redness within minutes, so the eyes look fresher for a while. A small trial has tested it for allergic eye itch.

lead: A cold compress for red eyes is the application of a chilled cloth, pack or similar object to the closed eyelids or face to reduce redness and puffiness for a short time. It is discussed as a quick appearance fix and as a comfort measure in some forms of eye irritation.

General references list many causes of red eye, from conjunctivitis to dry eye and blepharitis, and do not discuss cold compresses as a treatment for redness.[1] A small randomised trial has tested cold compresses in induced allergic conjunctivitis, and physiology research has examined how cold applied to the face affects autonomic responses such as heart rate and peripheral blood vessels.[2][3]
infobox: Allergic eye irritation, general eye comfort

paras: The approach uses a chilled object held against closed eyelids. Proponents describe it as a way to narrow blood vessels and reduce swelling quickly before photos or events.

Physiology research shows that cold applied to the face produces bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction, a response known as the diving reflex and used as a test of autonomic function.[3] That research concerns whole-body autonomic responses and not eye whiteness.

Wikipedia's article on conjunctivitis lists causes of red eye including viral, bacterial, allergic and chemical conjunctivitis, as well as corneal abrasion, dry eye, blepharitis, keratitis, uveitis and acute angle-closure glaucoma, the last being urgent.[1] It describes allergic cases as sometimes eased by artificial tears or antihistamines.[1]

A randomised, masked trial of 18 grass-pollen-allergic adults tested artificial tears and a cold compress, alone or in combination, after exposure in an environmental chamber, comparing them with topical antiallergic medication.[2] No studies found testing cold compresses for cosmetic eye whiteness in healthy people.
